title: Poson
hookLine: Sri Lanka's June full moon: Mahinda brings the teaching to the island

cards: A king is out hunting on a mountain, chasing a deer through the trees near his capital, the old city of Anuradhapura in Sri Lanka.
The deer leads him up a slope, and then, the chronicle says, a voice calls him by his name. Tissa. Not his title.
His name. Standing on a rock is a monk in robes, with companions, and the king has never seen anything like them.
Sri Lankans tell this story on the June full moon, the day they call Poson, more than two thousand years later. The mountain is Mihintale.

teach.b: The monk is Mahinda, and according to the Sri Lankan chronicles he's the son of Ashoka, the great Indian emperor who embraced the teaching. He has come, the chronicle says, to bring the Buddha's teaching to the island.
But first he tests the king, not with a sermon but with a riddle. What is this tree called? A mango, says the king.
Are there other mangoes besides this one? Many. And are there other trees besides this mango and the other mangoes?
Many, but those aren't mangoes. And besides the other mangoes and the trees that aren't mangoes?

teach.h: A RIDDLE ABOUT A MANGO TREE.

teach.b: Then he asks the same about the king's relatives, and others who are not his relatives, and the king answers that too. Mahinda is satisfied: this man can think. Only then does he teach.
The king, Devanampiya Tissa, comes to the teaching, and the chronicles describe the island turning toward it.
Later, Mahinda's sister, the nun Sanghamitta, is said to have brought a cutting from the Bodhi tree, and a tree at Anuradhapura grown from it is still honored today.
On Poson, pilgrims in white climb the long stairway at Mihintale, and families set up dansal along the roads, as at Vesak. Notice what the festival honors.
Not the Buddha's life this time, but the moment the teaching arrived somewhere new, carried by a person, starting with a question about a mango tree.

how: On Poson, Sri Lankan Buddhists make pilgrimage to Mihintale and Anuradhapura, dress in white, keep precepts, decorate streets with lanterns, and run dansal giving free food and drink.

o: a June harvest festival at Anuradhapura
the Sri Lankan festival of the Buddha's birth
Sri Lanka's June full moon, when the teaching arrived

p: monk, son of Ashoka by tradition

s: Mahinda began by preaching a long sermon to the king
he began with a riddle about a mango tree, to test the king's mind.
Poson falls on the June full moon in Sri Lanka
it remembers the teaching's arrival on the island.
the king was hunting a deer when he met Mahinda
the chronicle says the chase led him to Mihintale.

games.q: you're Mahinda, arriving to teach a king you've never met. what do you do first?
o: preach the four noble truths at once.
test his mind with a riddle about a mango tree.
ask him to build a monastery.
games.why: Mahinda asks about mango trees and relatives, step by step. satisfied that the king can reason, he teaches.

practice: Ask yourself how any of this reached you: the teachings, this path, the habit of sitting still. Was it a person, a book, a grandparent, a friend who mentioned it once, an app on a phone?
Let a face or a moment come, and let some thanks rise, in whatever form it takes.

wordCard.voice: Poson. Sri Lanka's June full moon, when the arrival of the teaching with Mahinda at Mihintale is remembered. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali Mahinda: the monk who, by Sri Lankan tradition, brought the teaching to the island.

carryVoice: Your line: who brought it. Every teaching arrives in someone's hands. Day six hundred eighty-three.
